To prevent the exception from being invoked abusively, new article 1221 was 
amended at the ratification stage in 2018 to require that the defaulting party must 
be acting in good faith for it to apply. This was intended to remove the possible 
incentive for a party to commit a breach of contract deliberately with a view to ar­
guing, in bad faith, that the cost of enforced performance is manifestly dispropor­
tionate to the interest of the injured party in obtaining the remedy.65
No guidance is provided in the reforms either as to the factors that are relevant 
to assessing the interest of the injured party or the meaning of ‘manifest dispropor­
tion’. Commentators have anticipated that relevant factors are likely to include the 
seriousness of the breach, the extent of the injured party’s loss, the level of difficulty 
obtaining the promised performance elsewhere, whether the injured party would 
themselves be in breach of a separate contract with a third party (for example where 
there are back-​to-​back contracts) and the risk of under-​compensation if compen­
satory damages were awarded.66 As for ‘manifest disproportion’, there is consensus 
that it must be blatant, in the sense of ‘certain, evident and flagrant’,67 which serves 
to limit the scope of the exception.68
Whether the exception will have a significant practical impact remains to be 
seen. It is widely expected to be interpreted narrowly by French courts, which his­
torically have been liberal in ordering specific enforcement.69 Such an approach 
would certainly be welcomed by French commentators, for whom enforced per­
formance should only be refused in extreme cases. In the words of Deshayes, 
Genicon, and Laithier, ‘the exception is not a principle that is in competition 
with the binding force of contract and the general availability of specific enforce­
ment. . . It would be a mistake to infer that specific enforcement will be ruled out 
every time compensatory damages are adequate to fulfil the expectations of the in­
jured party.’70 The same is true where a replacement can be obtained in the market­
place or the cost of the remedy is high. They have also said that ‘this limitation is 
meant to operate at the margin’,71 and is ‘exceptional’ in character.72
As well as introducing this exception, the reforms also removed a limitation on
